He asked me who I was tonight, politely, the way you'd ask a stranger holding your coat. In July my sister promised she'd take a weekend; it's October now and I've stopped asking. She calls me by her sister's name most evenings, and correcting her stopped feeling worth it around Easter. Filling out the intake form took longer than the crying did. Three weeks until the next opening, the coordinator said, and I laughed a little, because what else. When I finally said the ugly thing out loud, she didn't flinch, and her not flinching undid something in me. Sometimes I lock the bathroom door and run the fan, just to buy ninety seconds no one can interrupt. Fragile isn't the word; scraped clean is closer to how the drive home felt. Cancelled my own doctor's appointment twice this month because there was no one to sit with her. When did I last sleep through a whole night without listening for the door alarm? I kept staring at the box of tissues on her side table, daring myself not to need it. Told my sister it was a dentist appointment; that felt easier than explaining what it actually was. Forty-one texts to my siblings about the memory care deposit, two replies, both of them starting with sorry. Tired isn't the word anymore; it's something structural, like a beam sagging under a weight it was never rated for. Dad hid his blood pressure pills in the fern again, grinning like a boy who'd won something. At checkout the receptionist called me "hon" while photocopying my card, and I had to study the carpet for a second. I want to write a suicide letter.
